## Overview

The SEIR model has two infected compartments, exposed (`E`) and infectious (`I`), but
only one of them, `E`, can be entered by infection. This vignette shows the difference
between the next-generation matrix with *large domain* `K_L = -T Σ⁻¹`, indexed by all
infected states, and the next-generation matrix `K = Eᵀ K_L E` restricted to the
*states-at-infection*, which is what Diekmann et al. (2010) call *the* next-generation
matrix. Both have the same non-zero eigenvalues (this is proved in the package's Lean
formalisation, `proofs/ReproductiveNumbersProofs/Restriction.lean`), so both give `R₀`,
but `K` is smaller and its entries have a direct interpretation.

With births and deaths the infection-free steady state is unique and the package finds
it automatically.

## The model

```{julia}
using ReproductiveNumbers, ModelingToolkit, Symbolics
using ModelingToolkit: t_nounits as t, D_nounits as D

@parameters β σ γ μ N
@variables S(t) E(t) I(t) R(t)
eqs = [D(S) ~ μ * N - β * S * I / N - μ * S,
    D(E) ~ β * S * I / N - (σ + μ) * E,
    D(I) ~ σ * E - (γ + μ) * I,
    D(R) ~ γ * I - μ * R]
seir = complete(System(eqs, t; name = :seir))
```

## Infection-free steady state

Setting `E = I = 0` and solving the remaining equations gives `S = N`, `R = 0`:

```{julia}
disease_free_equilibrium(seir, [E, I])
```

## Transmissions and transitions

```{julia}
ngm = next_generation_matrix(seir, [E, I])
```

Only the first row of `T` is non-zero: new infections always appear in `E`. So `E` is the
only state-at-infection and the selection matrix `E` (the field `ngm.E`) has a single
column:

```{julia}
states_at_infection(ngm), ngm.E
```

`-Σ⁻¹` is the matrix of expected sojourn times. Its `(2, 1)` entry is the expected time
spent infectious by someone who is currently exposed: the probability `σ/(σ+μ)` of
surviving the latent period times the mean infectious period `1/(γ+μ)`.

```{julia}
-inv(ngm.Σ) .|> ReproductiveNumbers.tidy
```

## Large versus restricted domain

`K_L` tells us how many new infections an individual in *any* infected state will produce:
`K_L[1, 2] = β/(γ+μ)` for someone who is already infectious, and `K_L[1, 1]` for someone
just exposed, who must first survive the latent period.

```{julia}
ngm.K_L
```

Its second row is zero (nobody is *born* infectious), so the matrix is singular and its
non-zero spectrum is that of the `1 × 1` restriction:

```{julia}
ngm.K
```

```{julia}
R0 = basic_reproduction_number(ngm)
```

The characteristic polynomial of `K_L` makes the shared non-zero eigenvalue explicit:

```{julia}
characteristic_polynomial(ngm.K_L)
```

## Numeric check

```{julia}
using LinearAlgebra
p = Dict(β => 0.5, σ => 0.25, γ => 0.2, μ => 0.01, N => 1000.0)
num = evaluate(ngm, p)
(basic_reproduction_number(num), maximum(abs, eigvals(num.K_L)),
    Symbolics.value(substitute(R0, p)))
```

The sign conventions of van den Driessche & Watmough (2002) (`T ≥ 0`, `Σ` with
non-negative off-diagonal and non-positive diagonal entries, `-Σ⁻¹ ≥ 0`) can be checked
numerically:

```{julia}
validate_decomposition(num)
```

And `R₀ > 1` if and only if the Jacobian `T + Σ` of the infected subsystem has an
eigenvalue with positive real part:

```{julia}
maximum(real, eigvals(num.T + num.Σ))
```

## Choosing the infected states by name

Symbols work as well as symbolic variables, and the order of the infected states only
changes the ordering of rows and columns:

```{julia}
basic_reproduction_number(seir, [:I, :E])
```
